newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T indicated lower in pre-market trade.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T indicated lower in pre-market trade.

text.p: Shares in B.A.T. Industries Plc were indicated 22-1/2p lower to 466-1/2 by 0808 GMT in pre-market trade on Friday, following news late on Thursday that Liggett Group Inc had struck a legal settlement with 22 U.S. states.

News of the settlement which will require Liggett, the smallest major U.S. tobacco company to pay to U.S. states 25 percent of its pre-tax profits for the next 25 years sent tobacco shares in the U.S. lower on Thursday.
On the American Stock Exchange, the Tobacco Index dropped 6.79 points to 283.66, down 2.34 percent.

Many tobacco stock analysts on both sides of the Atlantic do not believe the Liggett settlement will force other U.S. tobacco companies, including B.A.T's Brown & Williamson unit to hammer out similar deals with U.S. states.
"As far as other companies are concerned this is just nonsense. They have been winning in the U.S. courts, not losing," said Tom Bennett, analyst at Banque Paribas.

Bennett dismissed suggestions that U.S. states would discover anything new in documents, supplied by Liggett, which could be used in a batch of court cases that have dogged the tobacco industry over the past few years.
"This is all hype. "I can't believe Liggett has documents which the other tobacco companies don't have," Bennett said.
He noted that under U.S. evidence "discovery" rules, U.S. tobacco companies have already provided a large quantity of documents to U.S. state legal authorities who are conducting the lawsuits.
"They(U.S. states) already have a warehouse that contains 20 million documents," Bennett said.
Liggest has been asked by the states to isolate the 25 most damaging documents.

Wall Street analysts said the settlement was a bald ploy by Brooke Group's chairman, Bennett LeBow, owner of Liggett, to coerce another tobacco company to acquire his company which has a two percent U.S. market share.

"The only real idea that makes sense is that(LeBow) is hopeful that, if he is enough of a thorn in the side of the industry, someone will buy him out to shut him down," said David Adelman, analyst at Dean Witter in New York.
Paribas Bennett, doubts B.A.T will try and negotiate a settlement with the U.S. states anytime soon, but he believes B.A.T would "jump at the chance" to cut the same deal that Liggett has done.
"The same terms would cost B.A.T $200 million a year. At the moment B.A.T is spending $100 million on legal costs alone," Bennett said.
"It would be worth it just to get the U.S. states off their backs."
B.A.T, which was indicated down 17-1/2p to 471-1/2p in the opening minutes, quickly hit a low of 460p but Bennett believes investors will buy on dips.
"B.A.T is yielding the same as gilts. The time to buy is just after news like this."
No one at B.A.T Industries was immediately available to comment.
